title: Quantum Secret Sharing from CSS qLDPC Codes: Computable Access Structures, Accessible Logical Dimension, and Topology-Aware Network Cost
abstract: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) schemes can be constructed from quantum error-correcting codes, but characterizing their access structures and implementation costs becomes challenging for finite-length, high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. We develop an exact computational framework for QSS induced by CSS qLDPC codes. The framework characterizes authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions using restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra, and introduces the accessible logical dimension \(κ(A)\), defined through the symplectic rank of locally supported logical classes, to refine the characterization of intermediate coalitions. We further incorporate physical network constraints through separate Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth costs, and treat the partitioning of physical qubits into participants as an explicit design variable. Numerical experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes verify the predicted complement duality and monotonicity properties and show substantial variation in access transitions and network costs. For the codes studied, the bivariate bicycle instance exhibits the sharpest transition, while network embedding costs vary by more than an order of magnitude across physical topologies. We also show that participant partitioning can substantially improve block-level security and reconstruction thresholds. These results provide a practical bridge between the algebraic structure of CSS qLDPC codes, the graded accessibility of quantum secrets, and the physical constraints of networked QSS implementations.
summary: This paper establishes a comprehensive computational framework for analyzing Quantum Secret Sharing derived from CSS qLDPC codes. It moves beyond pure algebra by quantifying physical implementation overheads, such as network routing and scheduling depth. The results show that the physical topology and qubit partitioning can significantly alter the achievable security and reconstruction thresholds of the quantum secret.
main_problem: The paper develops an exact computational framework to characterize Quantum Secret Sharing (QSS) access structures and incorporate physical implementation costs when using CSS quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes.
main_result: The framework successfully characterizes authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions using algebraic criteria, and demonstrates that physical network constraints (like Steiner-routing cost) significantly impact the practical security and reconstruction thresholds of the QSS scheme.
method: The methods involve using restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra to analyze the logical structure, alongside incorporating physical network costs (Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, scheduling-depth) as explicit design variables.
model_or_system: The system modeled is Quantum Secret Sharing implemented via CSS qLDPC codes. The security and accessibility are determined by the algebraic properties of the code's parity-check matrices ($H_X, H_Z$) and the structure of the resulting logical operators.
key_observables: Authorized/forbidden coalition status, accessible logical dimension $\kappa(A)$, total network cost ($W_{tot}$), Steiner-routing cost ($C_{St}$), and block-level security/reconstruction thresholds.
important_parameters: Code parameters (e.g., $[[72, 12, 6]]$), secret rate ($R_s$), and the physical topology of the network.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to using CSS qLDPC codes, and the network cost calculations rely on treating qubit partitioning as an explicit design variable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the block-level access profiles for different codes and partitions, and show the distribution of ramp width ($\Delta t$) over random balanced partitions, comparing these to theoretical benchmarks.
paper_structure: The paper builds from an algebraic characterization of QSS access structures using linear algebra (Chunk 2), extends this by introducing the accessible logical dimension $\kappa(A)$ (Chunk 1), and finally integrates physical network constraints and analyzes specific code families using numerical experiments (Chunks 3 & 4).
why_interesting: This work provides a highly detailed, computationally rigorous bridge connecting abstract algebraic coding theory (QEC) to the practical engineering challenges of implementing quantum protocols in physical, networked hardware.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Curves show Pauth, Pforb and Pint. The kL = 1 baseline is nearly a perfect threshold scheme, while the kL = 16 baseline is dominated by intermediate coalitions.

FIG. 2. Estimated access probabilities for the random sparse HGP code [[208, 20]]. The dashed vertical line marks the rate- dependent asymptotic erasure benchmark qcap = (1+Rs)/2 ≈ 0.548 of Eq. (80). The comparison is a finite-size diagnostic and carries no asymptotic capacity claim.

FIG. 3. Access probabilities for the bivariate bicycle code [[72, 12, 6]], obtained by exact enumeration where feasible and Monte Carlo sampling otherwise. The dashed line marks qcap = (1 + kL/n)/2 = 7/12 ≈0.583. The shaded band indi- cates the distance-guaranteed forbidden region a ≤d−1 = 5.

FIG. 4. Mean normalized accessible logical dimension κ(a)/kL against normalized coalition size for the codes with kL > 1. The quantity interpolates continuously between the forbidden regime (κ = 0) and the authorized regime (κ = kL), grading the intermediate family that the ternary classification of Theorem 9 leaves undifferentiated.

Controlled ensemble at n = 225 and Wtot = 1512: transition width ∆q, ramp area Aramp and secret rate Rs for 8 quasi-cyclic and 8 random biregular hypergraph-product in- stances with identical seed dimensions and weight profiles.
